html:
Bretton Woods was the conference held in July 1944 at a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, where 44 Allied nations agreed on rules for money and trade after the Second World War. It created the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, and a system of fixed exchange rates that lasted until the early 1970s.

The planners wanted to avoid the mistakes of the 1930s, when the Wall Street crash and the Great Depression had led countries to devalue their money against each other and shut out trade, feeding poverty and war. The two leading figures were the British economist John Maynard Keynes and the American official Harry Dexter White. The United States, which held most of the world's gold, largely got its way.

How it worked:

  • Each currency had a fixed rate against the US dollar.
  • The dollar was fixed to gold, at 35 dollars an ounce, and foreign governments could swap dollars for gold.
  • The IMF lent to countries in short-term trouble so they would not have to devalue.
  • The World Bank lent for rebuilding Europe and, later, for development in poorer countries.

This made the dollar the centre of world finance. The system helped bring the fastest growth in history in the 1950s and 1960s. But as US spending rose, foreigners held more dollars than the US had gold. In 1971 President Nixon stopped turning dollars into gold, and by 1973 the major currencies floated. The IMF and World Bank still exist, and the dollar is still the world's main reserve currency.
